lab.title: The Denials Pilot
lab.summary: Launch an AI denials-triage pilot with a skeptical billing team, a hard deadline and an auditor who is paying attention.
lab.role: You are the VP of Revenue Cycle at Harbor Point Regional Health (a composite organization: three hospitals in Ohio, 4,200 staff, Epic). You have $400,000 and twelve weeks. The CFO wants denials down 20% by Q3; your billing team has seen two automation projects fail.
lab.stakes: Recover cash without losing the billing team's trust or drawing a compliance finding. Every choice moves the dashboard.

start.title: Monday, 8:10 a.m.: how do you start?
start.body:
The vendor demo went well. The model flagged 71% of last quarter's preventable denials in a back test. Your billing manager, Dana Ortiz, is less impressed: "The last tool rewrote our appeal letters and we spent a month cleaning up."

The CFO's email is already in your inbox.

materials.body: I need a visible number by the board meeting in week 10. The vendor says we can switch on auto-submission for every denial code on day one. Is there a reason not to?

ending.title: Fast, then frozen
ending.body: The contractor's expanded review takes five months. The tool is switched off, $210,000 in payments are recouped, and the CFO asks for a full post-mortem.
ending.debrief: Speed without an evidence trail, then a response written by someone else, turned a routine records request into an audit. Accountability for claims stays with the hospital whatever the tool does.

path.nodeTitle: Monday, 8:10 a.m.: how do you start?
path.label: Switch on auto-submission for every code, as the vendor suggests
path.rationale: Fast, visible cash, but no human review, no baseline and no evidence trail. Automating submission before you know the error rate moves the risk to the payer and the auditor.
path.outcome: Corrected claims start flowing on day two. Cash comes in fast, and so do complaints: the billers find appeal letters they never saw going out under their names.

path.nodeTitle: Week 3, Thursday: how do you answer?
path.label: Let the vendor answer and tell the team to keep going
path.rationale: You are accountable for your claims, not the vendor. Letting a third party describe your controls, without checking, turned an inquiry into an audit.
path.outcome: The vendor's response describes a review step your hospital never performed. The contractor expands the request to every claim the tool touched.

expertPath.nodeTitle: Monday, 8:10 a.m.: how do you start?
expertPath.label: Start with the top 3 denial codes and a two-week shadow run beside the billers
expertPath.rationale: A shadow run builds evidence and trust at the same time, and it produces the audit trail you will need later. It costs two weeks, which the twelve-week window can absorb.
expertPath.outcome: Dana's team works their queue as usual while the model scores the same claims. By Friday of week two you have a side-by-side: the model agrees with the billers on 88% of claims and catches 140 they missed.

expertPath.nodeTitle: Week 3, Thursday: how do you answer?
expertPath.label: Send the shadow-run comparison as evidence of human review
expertPath.rationale: The shadow run you chose in week one was the evidence. Building the audit trail before you need it is the cheapest compliance control there is.
expertPath.outcome: Your two-week side-by-side shows every corrected claim was reviewed by a biller. The contractor closes the request in eleven days.

expertPath.nodeTitle: Week 6: the CFO wants to scale
expertPath.label: Scale to 10 codes, with weekly human review of a 5% sample
expertPath.rationale: Scaling in steps with a standing human sample keeps the speed and keeps the evidence. It is the pattern that survives the next audit.
expertPath.outcome: Seven more codes go live over two weeks. The weekly sample catches a drift in CO-50 decisions in week 8, which the team fixes before it reaches a payer.

expertPath.nodeTitle: Week 9: what do you tell the team?
expertPath.label: Make the billers the reviewers of record and fund two backfill roles from the recovered cash
expertPath.rationale: Naming the humans who stay in the loop, and paying for them, is how you keep the oversight that made the pilot work.
expertPath.outcome: The team hears that review is now their job title, not a side task. Two offers go out within the month.

principles:
Build the evidence trail before you need it: a shadow run is a trust exercise and a compliance control at once.

Accountability for AI-assisted decisions stays with the organization; never let a vendor describe controls you have not verified.

Scale in measured steps with a standing human sample, and treat the reviewers as part of the system, not a cost to remove.

realWorld.text: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0, January 2023) organizes AI risk work into four functions, Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, and treats human oversight and documentation as part of managing risk.
